lesson.title: Closing the Door: The Emergency Quota Act of 1921
lesson.summary: In 1921, Congress passed the first law placing hard numerical limits on immigration by nationality, a sharp break from the nation's traditionally open door and a direct outgrowth of postwar nativism.
lesson.body:
The nativist anxieties described in the previous chapter did not stay confined to public opinion and mob violence. They quickly translated into federal law. In May 1921, President Warren Harding signed the Emergency Quota Act, the first statute in American history to cap immigration using fixed numerical quotas tied to nationality.

The law's formula set each country's annual quota at 3 percent of the number of people from that country who were already living in the United States according to the 1910 census, with an overall ceiling of roughly 350,000 immigrants per year. Because the 1910 census still reflected decades of earlier immigration from Britain, Germany, and Scandinavia, those nations received comparatively generous quotas. Countries that had sent large numbers of immigrants only in the more recent New Immigration Wave, especially Italy, Poland, and Russia, saw their allowed numbers shrink dramatically compared to the levels of the previous two decades.

Congress framed the law as a temporary, emergency measure, meant to be revisited rather than a permanent fixture of immigration policy. But the political forces behind it, the nativist sentiment and Red Scare fears already reshaping public opinion, did not fade. Reformers who wanted even tighter and more permanent restrictions kept pushing, setting the stage for a stricter successor law only a few years later: the National Origins Act of 1924.
